native_result.query: What is the proportion of junior professors in replicated studies in Psychology?
native_result.HypoA: In Psychology, replicated studies have a much higher proportion of junior professor (64.7%) and in the original studies the senior professors are more represented (82.4%)
native_result.HypoB: In the Psychology replication project (project = "rpp"), 40.0% of the replicated studies (36 of 90 usable replication attempts; 95% Wilson interval 30.5-50.3%) were led by a junior professor - their most senior author being an Assistant Professor (22) or an Assistant (14) - so junior faculty ran roughly two in five RPP replications; the share rises to 51.6% (16/31) among the studies that actually replicated and is 39.2% (38/97) without the drop filter, and because "junior professor" is not a label in the data it is bounded between 15.6% (Assistant only) and 66.7% (also counting Associate Professors). Seniority is coded only for the most senior author of each team, so this is the share of studies led by junior faculty rather than a share of individual authors, and the original-study side shows no junior professors at all in rpp (Professor 76, Associate Professor 9, Researcher 5 of 90), so the figure describes the people who ran the replications. Descriptively, replication teams were far less senior than the originals they tested (mean author citations 463 vs 2,957) and junior-led attempts replicated at 44.4% versus 27.8% for the rest - a pattern in 90 studies, not evidence of an effect of seniority on replication success.
native_result.WorkflowB: File A (927 rows, study x lab) filtered to project=='rpp' (97 rows, one per study id), deduplicated by id, aggregated==True excluded (none in rpp; ml1/ml3 lab rows would have to be collapsed first), drop==True excluded (7 rows) -> n=90 usable replication attempts, no missing seniority. Junior professor = seniority.r in {Assistant Professor, Assistant}: 36/90 = 40.0% (Wilson 30.5-50.3%, Clopper-Pearson 29.8-50.9%). Parallel denominators: replicated==1 (16/31 = 51.6%) and all 97 rows (38/97 = 39.2%). Sensitivity grid across 3 rank definitions x 2 seniority columns x 3 denominators; seniority distribution table for both columns; discipline split (Cognitive 19/42 = 45.2%, Social 17/48 = 35.4%); descriptive context on replication success by rank and citation/author-count contrasts; light cross-check of rpp outcomes against File B on 63 unambiguously matched ids (100% outcome agreement, corr(log10 p)=0.999), which does not alter the estimate. Headline figures independently re-derived with a separate raw-csv parse.

sub_hypo.text: Junior faculty led 40.0% of usable Psychology replication attempts (36/90): 22 teams had an Assistant Professor and 14 an Assistant as their most senior author.

sub_hypo.relations: Junior-led means seniority.r is Assistant Professor or Assistant; 36/90=40.0%, with a 95% Wilson interval of 30.5–50.3% and Clopper–Pearson interval of 29.8–50.9%.

sub_hypo.context: The 31 successful replications among the 90 usable RPP attempts, after deduplication and exclusion of aggregated=True and drop=True.

sub_hypo.text: The estimated share of junior-led RPP replications ranges from 15.6% to 66.7% depending on which seniority ranks count as junior.
sub_hypo.context: The 90 usable RPP replication attempts; 'junior professor' is not a data label, and rank refers to each team's most senior author.
sub_hypo.relations: Counting only Assistants gives 15.6%; counting Assistants and Assistant Professors gives 40.0%; additionally counting Associate Professors gives 66.7%.

sub_hypo.text: The original RPP studies had no junior-led teams under the Assistant Professor-or-Assistant definition, unlike the replication teams.
sub_hypo.context: The 90 usable RPP original–replication study pairs, deduplicated and excluding aggregated=True and drop=True.
sub_hypo.relations: Original-team seniority was Professor in 76 studies, Associate Professor in nine, and Researcher in five, with no Assistants or Assistant Professors; replication teams included 36 junior-led studies.

sub_hypo.text: Replication teams were descriptively less senior than the original teams they tested, with lower mean author citations.
sub_hypo.context: The 90 usable RPP original–replication study pairs.
sub_hypo.relations: Replication teams had mean author citations of 463 versus 2,957 for original teams, alongside the descriptive seniority contrast.

sub_hypo.text: Junior-led RPP replication attempts succeeded more often than other attempts, descriptively rather than causally.

sub_hypo.relations: Junior-led attempts replicated at 44.4%, versus 27.8% for other attempts; this is not evidence that seniority affects replication success.
